The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Under this assumption Lebesgue measure is the completion of Borel measure ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]), and every Lebesgue-measurable integrable class has a Borel representative ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]]). Write $\lambda_3$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a positive reference speed $v_0>0$, and put $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$. Let $X$ be the real vector space of equivalence classes modulo $\lambda_3$-almost-everywhere equality of measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with

$$\|f\|_{1,w_0}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_0(v)|f(v)|\,d\lambda_3(v)<\infty.$$

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$. For a Borel set $E\subseteq S^2$, define the normalized finite angular measure

$$\sigma(E):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf 1_E(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\phi\,d\theta.$$

For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in S^2$, define the postcollision velocities

$$v'=v-((v-w)\cdot n)n,\qquad w'=w+((v-w)\cdot n)n.$$

The collision-parameter measure is $d\mu=d\lambda_3(v)\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Its angular factor is finite and normalized; there is no singular angular weight. For $f,g\in X$, choose Borel representatives and define the gain $\mathcal G(f,g)$ by the almost-everywhere integral

$$\mathcal G(f,g)(v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3\times S^2} f(v')g(w')\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n).$$

The value on any exceptional null set is immaterial because the output is an equivalence class. The next item proves that this definition is independent of the representatives, maps $X\times X$ to $X$, and has the stated collision and moment identities.

and then $\lambda_n(E) = \beta_n(A)$.

derivations.claim: Put $c=(v+w)/2$ and $r=(v-w)/2$. The formulas in [F1] give $v'=c+r-2(r\cdot n)n$ and $w'=c-r+2(r\cdot n)n$. The map $r\mapsto r-2(r\cdot n)n$ is reflection across the plane perpendicular to $n$: applying it twice returns $r$, and its squared norm is $|r|^2$. The center $c$ is fixed. Hence the pair map is an orthogonal involution on $\mathbb R^6$, its determinant has absolute value one, $v'+w'=v+w$, and $|v'|^2+|w'|^2=|v|^2+|w|^2$.

The defining integral of $\sigma$ has total mass $(4\pi)^{-1}(2)(2\pi)=1$. Every nonempty relative-open subset of $S^2$ contains a patch away from a coordinate pole and seam; its preimage contains an open rectangle on which $\sin\theta>0$, so it has positive $\sigma$-measure. Every nonempty open subset of the full parameter space contains a product of two Euclidean balls and such a sphere patch; each factor has positive measure, so $\mu$ has full support. For an elastic pair, set $c=(v+w)/2$, $r=(v-w)/2$, and $\tilde r=(\tilde v-\tilde w)/2$. Momentum and squared-speed conservation give the same center and $|\tilde r|=|r|$. If $\tilde r\ne r$, choose $n=(r-\tilde r)/|r-\tilde r|$; the equal-norm identity gives $2(r\cdot n)n=r-\tilde r$, hence the reflection sends $r$ to $\tilde r$. If $\tilde r=r$, choose any unit $n$ perpendicular to $r$ when $r\ne0$, and any unit $n$ when $r=0$. Thus every elastic pair is attained.

Replace the representatives of $f$ and $g$ by Borel representatives using [F2]. Tonelli [F3] makes the sections measurable and permits integration in any order. For each fixed $n$, the pair reflection in step 1.1 is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with unit absolute Jacobian, so [F4] gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^6} h(v',w')\,dv\,dw=\int_{\mathbb R^6}h(v,w)\,dv\,dw.$$ It follows that $\int |\mathcal G(f,g)|\,dv\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_1$. The same change of variables shows that altering either representative on a Lebesgue-null set changes the integrand only on a $\mu$-null set; therefore the output class is independent of representatives. Bilinearity follows from linearity of the integral. Since $|v|^2\le |v'|^2+|w'|^2$, one has $w_0(v)\le w_0(v')+w_0(w')$. Applying Tonelli and [F4] again gives $$\|\mathcal G(f,g)\|_{1,w_0}\le \|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g\|_1+\|f\|_1\|g\|_{1,w_0}\le2\|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g\|_{1,w_0}.$$ The same bounds applied to $|f|,|g|$ define the signed bilinear extension.

For $f\ge0$, use Tonelli and the unit-Jacobian involution to obtain $\int\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=\int f(v)f(w)\,dv\,dw=M^2$. For the first moment, the same change of variables gives $\int v\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=\int v'f(v)f(w)\,d\mu$. The simultaneous exchange $(v,w,n)\mapsto(w,v,n)$ preserves $\mu$ and swaps $v'$ with $w'$, while $f(v)f(w)$ is unchanged. Averaging the two expressions replaces $v'$ by $(v'+w')/2=(v+w)/2$, yielding $M\int vf\,dv$. Applying the same averaging to the second moment uses $(|v'|^2+|w'|^2)/2=(|v|^2+|w|^2)/2$ and gives $M\int|v|^2f\,dv$.

Let $M=1$ and let $\varphi$ satisfy the absolute-integrability conditions in the Statement. By [F4], $\int\varphi(v)\mathcal G(f,f)(v)\,dv=\int\varphi(v')A\,d\mu$. The incoming/outgoing involution sends $A$ to $B$ and $\Delta\varphi$ to $-\Delta\varphi$, so $\int(B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu=-2\int A\Delta\varphi\,d\mu$. Combining these equalities gives the claimed factor $1/4$ identity.

derivations.claim: By [F3], diagonalize $\Sigma$ in an orthonormal basis with eigenvalues $s_1^2,s_2^2,s_3^2\in[a,b]$. The linear substitution $y_i=(v-u)_i/s_i$ has Jacobian $\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}$; [F4] in each coordinate gives $\int\gamma_{\Sigma,u}(v)\,dv=1$. The same eigenvalue bounds give $(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\in[b^{-3/2},a^{-3/2}]$ and $|v-u|^2/b\le(v-u)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)\le|v-u|^2/a$, proving the two Gaussian envelopes for each component and hence for every finite mixture.

Let $O_n:\mathbb R^6\to\mathbb R^6$ be the orthogonal pair map from [F2], and let $P:\mathbb R^6\to\mathbb R^3$ project onto the first component. For component densities $\gamma_{\Sigma,u}$ and $\gamma_{\Tau,u}$, the joint centered covariance is $S=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma,\Tau)$. Using [F6] under $O_n$, the density of the pair after reflection is the centered Gaussian with covariance $S_n=O_nSO_n^{\mathsf T}$ and mean $(u,u)$. Write $S_n$ in blocks as $\begin{pmatrix}C&D\\D^{\mathsf T}&E\end{pmatrix}$. Its first marginal is Gaussian with covariance $C$: indeed $C$ is positive definite, the Schur complement $H=E-D^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}D$ is positive definite, and block elimination gives $\det S_n=\det C\det H$ and $$(x,y)^{\mathsf T}S_n^{-1}(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}x+(y-D^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}x)^{\mathsf T}H^{-1}(y-D^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}x).$$ Integrating in $y$ using [F3], [F4], and [F7] gives the normalized marginal $\gamma_{C,u}$. Also $C=PS_nP^{\mathsf T}$ satisfies $aI\le C\le bI$: for every $z$, $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=(z,0)^{\mathsf T}O_nSO_n^{\mathsf T}(z,0)$ lies between $a|z|^2$ and $b|z|^2$.

Differentiating a component $\gamma_{\Sigma,u}$ in $v$ multiplies it by a polynomial in $\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)$; each coefficient is uniformly bounded because $\|\Sigma^{-1}\|\le a^{-1}$. The exponent has the upper bound from step 1.1, so every derivative of a finite mixture has the stated polynomial-Gaussian envelope, uniformly over all finite mixtures in this class.

Therefore $\mathcal G(\gamma_{\Sigma,u},\gamma_{\Tau,u})$ is the pointwise angular average $\int_{S^2}\gamma_{C_n,u}\,d\sigma(n)$ with $C_n\in K_{a,b}$. The map $n\mapsto C_n$ is continuous, and $C\mapsto\gamma_{C,u}$ is continuous in $X$: pointwise convergence follows from the formula, while the weighted upper Gaussian envelope from step 1.1 is an integrable dominator and [F5] gives weighted-$L^1$ convergence. For each $n$, continuity supplies a relative-open neighborhood on which the $X$-distance from $\gamma_{C_n,u}$ is less than $\varepsilon$; compactness of $S^2$ gives a finite subcover. Successively subtracting earlier open sets makes this a finite Borel partition $E_j$, and choosing one $n_j$ in each nonempty piece gives variation at most $2\varepsilon$ on that piece. Tonelli [F7] and the triangle inequality bound the weighted-$L^1$ distance from the angular average to $\sum_j\sigma(E_j)\gamma_{C_{n_j},u}$ by $2\varepsilon\sum_j\sigma(E_j)=2\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, the angular average belongs to $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$. Bilinear expansion proves the same for finite convex mixtures in both inputs.

For general $f,g\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$, choose finite-mixture sequences $f_k\to f$ and $g_k\to g$ in $X$. The bound [F2] gives $$\|\mathcal G(f_k,g_k)-\mathcal G(f,g)\|_{1,w_0}\le2\|f_k-f\|_{1,w_0}\|g_k\|_{1,w_0}+2\|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g_k-g\|_{1,w_0}\longrightarrow0.$$ Each $\mathcal G(f_k,g_k)$ is in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ by step 2.2, so closedness proves $\mathcal G(f,g)\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$.

Let $f_k$ be finite mixtures converging in $X$ to $f\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$. By step 2.1, every derivative sequence $(\partial^\alpha f_k)_k$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on every closed ball, since the next derivatives have a common bound there. On the countable dense rational grid in each ball, bounded real sequences admit convergent subsequences: repeatedly bisect a bounded interval, retain a half containing infinitely many terms, and use the nested intervals of lengths tending to zero to select a convergent subsequence. A countable diagonal selection over grid points, integer-radius balls, and multi-indices makes every derivative converge on every grid. Equicontinuity and a finite rational $\delta$-net of each ball then make these subsequences uniformly Cauchy there, hence locally uniformly convergent. The fundamental theorem of calculus along coordinate segments identifies the limits as derivatives of a smooth function $\widetilde f$. Weighted-$L^1$ convergence identifies $\widetilde f=f$ almost everywhere on every ball, so $\widetilde f$ represents $f$. The pointwise envelopes and derivative bounds pass to the local uniform limit. This proves part 1 for every class element.

To prove $X$ complete, let $(g_n)$ be Cauchy in its norm and choose a subsequence $(g_{n_j})$ with $\|g_{n_{j+1}}-g_{n_j}\|_{1,w_0}\le2^{-j}$. By [F5], the nonnegative series $\sum_j w_0|g_{n_{j+1}}-g_{n_j}|$ is finite almost everywhere and has finite integral. Hence $g_{n_j}$ converges pointwise almost everywhere to a measurable $g$, and the integral of each tail is bounded by $\sum_{j\ge J}2^{-j}$, so $g_{n_j}\to g$ in $X$. The same estimates give $\|g\|_{1,w_0}<\infty$. Since the original sequence was Cauchy, it converges to the same $g$. Thus $X$ is complete.

It is closed: if $g_n\to g$ in $X$, then $\int|g_n-g|\le\|g_n-g\|_{1,w_0}$, $\int|v||g_n-g|\le(v_0/2)\|g_n-g\|_{1,w_0}$, and $\int|v|^2|g_n-g|\le v_0^2\|g_n-g\|_{1,w_0}$; also the negative part of $g$ is bounded by $|g-g_n|$ whenever $g_n\ge0$. Thus all constraints pass to the limit, and $K$ is complete. The continuous path space $C([0,T],K)$ with the supremum metric is complete: a uniformly Cauchy sequence has pointwise limits in $K$, converges uniformly, and the triangle inequality with one continuous approximant proves continuity of the limit.

Its Riemann sums are Cauchy in $X$ by uniform continuity on $[0,T]$ and completeness from step 1.1. The gain identities in [F2] show that $\Phi(g)_t$ has mass $1$, first moment $m_1$, and second moment $E_2$, since $e^{-\lambda t}+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}ds=1$; nonnegativity is preserved as well. The same upper Gaussian envelope holds for $\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)$ because [F3] preserves the mixture class; [F4] therefore bounds $|\partial_t f_t|$ by a constant times that envelope. The lower and upper bounds imply $|\log(v_0^3f_t(v))|\le C_1(1+|v-u|^2)$, after changing the finite constant $C_1$. Thus $f_t|\log(v_0^3f_t)|$ is integrable and the entropy derivative integrand has an integrable polynomial-Gaussian majorant on every compact time interval.

For each fixed $v$, the ordinary chain rule gives $\partial_t[f_t\log(v_0^3f_t)]=(1+\log(v_0^3f_t))\partial_t f_t$. The uniform majorant from step 1.1 also bounds the difference quotients by the scalar mean-value theorem. Dominated convergence [F5] therefore gives $H'(t)=\int(1+\log(v_0^3f_t))\partial_t f_t\,dv$. The mass of $f_t$ is constant by [F4], so $\int\partial_t f_t\,dv=0$ and the constant term drops. The integrand in the resulting formula is pointwise continuous in time by [F4] and has the same local integrable majorant from step 1.1; a second application of [F5] shows that $H'(t)$ is continuous.

Fix $t$ and write $\varphi(v)=\log(v_0^3f_t(v))$. The lower Gaussian bound makes $\varphi$ finite. The mean of $f_t$ is still $u$ by the moment conservation in [F4]. Also $A,B$ are bounded above by a constant times $e^{-(|v-u|^2+|w-u|^2)/(2b)}$, because the pair reflection fixes the common mean $(u,u)$ and preserves the sum of the two centered squared speeds. The Gaussian lower bound gives $|\log(A/B)|\le C_2(1+|v-u|^2+|w-u|^2)$, so all weak-form and entropy-production integrals converge absolutely. By [F2] and [F4],
$$H'(t)=\frac{\lambda}{4}\int(B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu.$$
The reference factors cancel in the logarithm: $\Delta\varphi=\log(A/B)$. Hence $H'(t)=-\frac{\lambda}{4}\int(B-A)\log(B/A)\,d\mu$. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, $(B-A)\log(B/A)\ge0$, proving the inequality.

If $H'(t)=0$, the continuous nonnegative integrand in step 3.1 vanishes $\mu$-almost everywhere. The product measure has full support by [F2]; a continuous function nonzero at one point is bounded away from zero on a nonempty open neighborhood of positive measure. Thus $A=B$ for every $(v,w,n)$. Conversely, this pointwise identity makes the production integral zero.

Put $g(v)=\log(v_0^3f_t(v))$, a $C^2$ function by [F3]. By the reflection coverage in [F2], for every center $c\in\mathbb R^3$ and every pair $r,r'\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|r|=|r'|$, the equality in step 4.1 gives $g(c+r)+g(c-r)=g(c+r')+g(c-r')$. For unit vectors $\theta,\eta$, take $r=s\theta$ and $r'=s\eta$. Taylor expansion at $c$ yields $g(c+s\theta)+g(c-s\theta)=2g(c)+s^2\theta^{\mathsf T}D^2g(c)\theta+o(s^2)$, with the same expression for $\eta$. Dividing by $s^2$ and taking $s\to0$ shows that the quadratic form of $D^2g(c)$ is constant on the unit sphere. Testing $e_i$ and $(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2$ shows $D^2g(c)=\alpha(c)I$.

The off-diagonal Hessian entries vanish, so for each $i$, $\partial_i g$ depends only on its $i$th coordinate: changing any other coordinate leaves it fixed by the fundamental theorem of calculus along that coordinate segment. Write $\partial_i g(v)=G_i(v_i)$. The equal diagonal entries give $G_i'(v_i)=G_j'(v_j)$ for independently variable coordinates $v_i,v_j$; hence every such derivative is one constant $\alpha$. Integrating gives $g(v)=c_0+\beta\cdot v+\frac{\alpha}{2}|v|^2$.

Integrability of $f_t=e^{g}/v_0^3$ forces $\alpha<0$: if $\alpha>0$ the density grows in every sufficiently large direction, and if $\alpha=0$ an exponential of an affine function is nonintegrable on $\mathbb R^3$. Completing the square writes $f_t=C e^{-|v-\bar u|^2/(2s^2)}$ with $s^2=-1/\alpha>0$; Tonelli [F7] and the one-dimensional Gaussian integral [F6] give $\int e^{-|v-\bar u|^2/(2s^2)}dv=(2\pi s^2)^{3/2}$, so unit mass fixes the prefactor in the Statement. Conversely, for that Gaussian $\log f_t$ is a constant plus a linear function of $v$ and a scalar multiple of $|v|^2$; pair momentum and squared-speed conservation in [F2] give $A=B$ at every collision. Define $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=1,0,-1$ according as $x>0,x=0,x<0$, and set $\varphi=\operatorname{sgn}(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t)$. This test is bounded and measurable; since $\int A\,d\mu=\int B\,d\mu=1$, both sides of the weak identity are absolutely integrable. Applying [F2] gives $\|\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t\|_1=0$. The constant curve satisfies the mild equation because $e^{-\lambda t}+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}ds=1$, and uniqueness in [F4] makes this Gaussian stationary.

The density formula in [F3] factors for $aI$ and $bI$ into products of one-dimensional Gaussians; Tonelli [F7] and normalization [F6] give the first-coordinate marginal as their equal mixture. For a centered one-dimensional Gaussian of variance $s^2$, integration of the derivative of $x^{2k-1}e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}$ over $\mathbb R$ gives $\int x^{2k}e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}dx=(2k-1)s^2\int x^{2k-2}e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}dx$ for $k=1,2$; the boundary terms vanish by Gaussian decay. Thus the mixture's centered second moment is $(a+b)/2$ and its fourth moment is $3(a^2+b^2)/2$. A single Gaussian with the same second moment has fourth moment $3((a+b)/2)^2$, smaller by $3(a-b)^2/4>0$. Thus $f_0$ is not a single Gaussian. By the equality characterization in steps 4.1–7.1, the production at $t=0$ is strictly positive and $H'(0)<0$.

For this selected model, an identical classical particle is nonrelativistic in the explicit sense that its velocity is a vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ and its kinetic energy is the Newtonian scalar $m|v|^2/2$. The mass $m>0$ is a primitive model parameter in kilograms. At time $t\ge0$, $f_t(v)$ is the probability density of velocity for a randomly selected particle with respect to Lebesgue measure $dv$; it is nonnegative, normalized by $\int f_t\,dv=1$, and therefore has SI units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the completed Lebesgue measure used by the mathematical gain definition ([[def-countable-choice]]). A positive speed $v_0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is a reference scale used only to make the logarithm in the one-particle information functional dimensionless. The Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ is a primitive conversion factor when that functional is assigned entropy units.

Adopt the spatially homogeneous kinetic equation

$$\partial_t f_t(v)=\lambda\bigl(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)(v)-f_t(v)\bigr),\qquad \lambda>0,$$

where $\mathcal G$ and the elastic reflection $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ are exactly those of [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] and [[lem-csm-dk-reflection-measure-and-gain-identities]]. The angular measure is the finite normalized area law specified there, and $\lambda$ is a prescribed rate in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, independent of relative speed; it is not a measured cross-section or a derived microscopic frequency. The selected incoming pair law is $f(v)f(w)\,dv\,dw$, and the gain uses the corresponding product $f(v')f(w')$ after reflection. This factorized independent-pair closure is adopted here; it is not deduced from reversible many-particle mechanics or from a molecular-chaos theorem. The mathematical existence and regularity claims are separate from this physical adoption.

The model's global mild evolution and its finite-energy hypotheses are mathematical claims treated separately from this physical adoption. This postulate makes no claim of a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, generic gas applicability, spatially inhomogeneous PDE well-posedness, a hydrodynamic limit, or observed entropy increase.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $v_0>0$, $\lambda>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$. Let

$$f_0(v)=\tfrac12\gamma_{aI,u}(v)+\tfrac12\gamma_{bI,u}(v),$$

and let $f_t$ be its global solution from [[thm-csm-dk-global-cutoff-collision-evolution]]. Define the dimensionless one-particle functional

$$H(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_t(v)\log(v_0^3f_t(v))\,dv.$$

For every $t\ge0$, $H$ is finite and continuously differentiable, and with $A=f_t(v)f_t(w)$ and $B=f_t(v')f_t(w')$,

$$H'(t)=-\frac{\lambda}{4}\int_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2}(B-A)\log(B/A)\,d\mu\le0.$$

The integrand is nonnegative. Equality holds at a time $t$ exactly when $f_t$ is a normalized isotropic Gaussian

$$f_t(v)=(2\pi s^2)^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|v-\bar u|^2}{2s^2}\right)$$

for some $\bar u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $s>0$; every such Gaussian is stationary. The specified initial mixture is not a single Gaussian, so $H'(0)<0$.
